frameworks.name: Six-Week Onboarding Challenge
frameworks.definition: A front-end offer structure for membership-based fitness businesses where new clients pay a premium upfront for a defined 6-week outcome program with a money-back or credit guarantee, which filters committed buyers, liquidates CAC via supplement sales, and converts to annual recurring membership via a mid-program upsell.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when a fitness business owner believes they are cash-constrained, the true cause is typically an underpriced front-end offer rather than insufficient cash: a customer acquisition cost of 200-250 euros with a monthly price of 80 euros per member means the offer itself is the structural problem, not the cash position.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When CAC exceeds first-month revenue, running ads drains cash; the correct diagnosis is that the front-end price is too low relative to acquisition cost, not that advertising must stop.

numbers.axis: Customer acquisition cost vs. monthly member price

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a fitness business can resolve a negative-CAC problem by introducing a paid onboarding program (he calls it an on-ramp or onboard) priced at approximately 600 euros for six weeks, replacing a free or low-friction entry with a commitment-qualifying front-end that covers the cost of acquisition before the member enters the regular membership.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi prescribes selling 200-300 euros worth of supplements during the initial nutrition consultation of the six-week onboarding challenge, which covers two months of product usage and is sufficient to fully liquidate the business's customer acquisition cost, eliminating the need for additional sessions to break even on ad spend.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: CAC of 200-250 euros via Facebook ads
claims.mechanism: Selling 3-4 supplement products covering two months of supply upfront captures the full CAC in a single transaction, making ad spend self-liquidating and restoring cash flow without requiring session revenue to recoup.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi advises personal training businesses to raise their standard monthly membership price from 80 euros to 130 euros and apply the 50-euro/month difference as a 12-month credit toward the six-week onboarding fee (600 euros), so that long-term members effectively pay their original 80 euros/month, while new customers can prepay for the remaining 10 months at a discounted rate of approximately 1,000 euros to lock in the year.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Six-week onboarding challenge at 600 euros introduced
claims.mechanism: Raising list price to 130 euros then crediting 50 euros/month for 12 months nets to 80 euros/month for continuing members while justifying a higher perceived value; it also frames the year prepay as a financial reward for commitment, anchoring the 600-euro onboarding cost against a year of full-price service.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the mid-program upsell pitch inside a six-week challenge should be delivered at the three-week mark, not at the end of the program, because waiting until the end of a challenge to pitch continuity sacrifices momentum and the client's peak emotional engagement.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Six-week fitness challenge with money-back or credit guarantee

numbers.axis: Timing of continuity upsell within a 6-week program

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for fitness businesses whose owners are not naturally skilled on camera, static image ads outperform video ads in Facebook advertising performance, but high-quality video with multiple clients working out in unison outperforms static ads when the operator can execute it well.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Facebook advertising for fitness/personal training businesses
Based on data from Gym Launch team (as of transcript recording)
bounded_by: Does not apply when operator is skilled on camera, where quality video outperforms static

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that fitness businesses running Facebook ads use video showing multiple clients performing the same exercise simultaneously (e.g., sit-ups, push-ups, jumping jacks in unison) as their highest-attention creative format, because synchronized movement is visually striking and attention-grabbing in a feed environment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Operator is able to coordinate group sessions for filming
claims.mechanism: Synchronized physical movement in video is a pattern-interrupt in social media feeds, drawing viewer attention before they scroll past; the offer details are placed in the copy rather than the video itself.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi reframes the primary objections of the 45-65 fitness demographic (Angelo's target audience) as fear of injury and lack of accountability, not weight-loss aspiration, asserting that the offer and program structure should be built around safety protocols and financial commitment mechanics that address those two fears, rather than aesthetic outcome promises.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Personal training business targeting 45-65 year old clientele
80% of clientele in the 45-55 to 65 range
bounded_by: Applies specifically to the 45-65 demographic; weight-loss framing may be appropriate for younger audiences

claims.text: Alex Hormozi demonstrates that a personal training business with three locations at 80 euros/member/month would need approximately 900 total members (300 per location) to reach 1 million euros in annual revenue, and that the business's inability to reach 1 million is a function of member volume, not price, requiring lead generation infrastructure rather than price increases alone.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Group personal training model (6 clients per hour)

numbers.axis: Members required per location to reach 1M annual revenue

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a personal trainer using direct outreach (WhatsApp, personal DMs) can acquire approximately 10 new customers per day if doing the outreach themselves, which at 30 days represents a viable path to 300 new members per location without paid ads.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Using AI-assisted WhatsApp or DM outreach to old leads and lapsed members

numbers.axis: Daily new customer acquisition via personal outreach

bounded_by: Assumes founder is personally executing outreach, not delegated to a team

claims.text: Alex Hormozi frames the mid-program continuity pitch for fitness challenges around rolling the upfront onboarding investment toward a year-long membership, positioning the pitch as matching the client's demonstrated commitment rather than as a sales transaction.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Three weeks into a six-week onboarding challenge
claims.mechanism: Framing the upsell as 'matching your commitment' reframes the commercial transaction as reciprocity, reducing resistance; crediting the onboarding fee toward the year removes financial friction and the anchor of 'I already paid' is leveraged rather than ignored.

examples.text: Angelo, the personal trainer being coached, runs three locations in Europe charging 80 euros/month for 20-minute group sessions (6 clients per trainer per hour, 4 sessions per month per member). Location 1 has 180 members, Location 2 has 46, and Location 3 has 105 — totaling roughly 331 members and 300k euros in annual revenue. He was running Facebook ads with a CAC of 200-250 euros, stopped due to perceived cash constraints, and switched to WhatsApp outreach using AI. Hormozi diagnosed the cash constraint as a front-end pricing problem: 250-euro CAC against an 80-euro first-month yield creates a 3+ month payback period, making ad spend appear unsustainable. The fix prescribed was a 600-euro six-week onboarding challenge plus supplement sales to achieve same-day CAC recovery.

Hormozi demonstrated the mid-challenge continuity pitch verbatim: at week three, the trainer says to the client: 'You've been showing up every time you said you were going to, and hopefully you feel like I did too. I'm going to take that money you put toward this and roll it toward the year, so we can make this a lifestyle rather than a quick diet. How does that sound? You want to prepay for the year right now? That's what most people do.' This script frames the credit of the onboarding fee as an act of reciprocity from the trainer, creates social proof with 'that's what most people do,' and avoids a hard close framing. Hormozi noted he had taught this script to 6,000 gym owners.

Angelo initially resisted the goal-based money-back guarantee component of the six-week challenge because his 45-65 year-old clientele do not primarily want to lose 20 pounds — they want to tone up and feel good. Hormozi responded that the goal itself is interchangeable; what matters is having a measurable, trackable goal to attach the accountability mechanic to. He suggested measuring body fat percentage at intake and at week six: even if weight stays the same, changing the body composition numbers gives the client a target and the trainer a proof point, converting a subjective goal (feel better) into a trackable metric that supports the continuity pitch.

practices.text: Read Gym Launch Secrets by Alex Hormozi before implementing a fitness business sales system; the book provides the full framework for running onboarding challenges and pricing structures for gym-format businesses.

During the initial nutrition consultation for the onboarding challenge, sell supplements upfront for the full six-week duration (two months of product), with 3-4 products recommended per client, to immediately cover your Facebook ad CAC in a single transaction.

For fitness businesses advertising on Facebook, if you are not comfortable on camera, test static image ads before attempting video; if you do use video, film multiple clients performing the same exercise in unison (synchronized movement) to maximize scroll-stopping attention.

When running a six-week onboarding challenge, measure and record client body fat percentage at the start and at week six so progress is trackable regardless of the client's aesthetic goal, creating a concrete metric to anchor the continuity upsell.

Deliver the continuity upsell pitch at week three of the six-week challenge, not at the end; pitch it as rolling the client's onboarding investment toward a year membership to make fitness a lifestyle.
